tagline: Stone bridges and tollhouses trace the first federally funded interstate highway.
intro: The Historic National Road links mountain driving in Maryland and Pennsylvania with Indiana’s farmland and pike towns. Near Pennsylvania’s Chestnut Ridge, US 40 has steep grades and sharp curves. The Federal Highway Administration lists this six-state All-American Road at 824.15 miles and allows two and a half days simply to drive it. Its account emphasizes the roadside inns, tollhouses, diners and motels that trace two centuries of American travel.

President Thomas Jefferson authorized the road west from Cumberland in 1806; construction began in 1811 and reached Wheeling in 1818. Congress funded extensions across Ohio and Indiana into Illinois, but federal construction stopped at Vandalia in 1839. Illinois did not continue the project without federal money because state roads already linked Vandalia with the St. Louis area. Today’s byway extends beyond the original federal road: Maryland’s itinerary begins in Baltimore, and Illinois’s ends in East St. Louis.

Travel west from Baltimore through Frederick and Cumberland to Casselman Bridge near Grantsville. Continue through Pennsylvania toward Uniontown and Brownsville, then Wheeling at the Ohio River. Across Ohio, the route passes Zanesville, Columbus and Springfield before Richmond, Indianapolis and Terre Haute in Indiana. Illinois carries the journey through Vandalia and onward to East St. Louis.

moments.title: Casselman Bridge
moments.text: Casselman Bridge’s stone arch spans eighty feet across the river near Grantsville. Built in 1813–1814 for the National Road, it carried traffic that included twelve-horse teams pulling ten-ton loads. The crossing was strengthened for motor vehicles in 1911, then superseded as a highway by a nearby steel bridge in 1933. Vehicle use ended in 1953, and state restoration followed. Maryland’s tourism office describes the old span as the connection between a state park and Spruce Forest Artisan Village. At the stone bridge’s approaches, small stretches of the original National Road remain.
moments.notice: Original National Road approaches lead to the stone arch.

moments.title: Wheeling Suspension Bridge
moments.text: The Wheeling Suspension Bridge crosses the Ohio River’s main channel from the city shore to Wheeling Island. Charles Ellet Jr. designed the bridge and supervised its construction; completed in 1849, it joined the eastern and western sections of the National Road. Its deck has changed since that first crossing. A windstorm destroyed it in May 1854, and Ellet’s workers made temporary repairs in eight weeks before further improvements. The main span measures 1,010 feet between its towers. Wikipedia’s bridge history records a permanent motor-vehicle ban announced by the state highway division in February 2026.

moments.title: Vandalia State House
moments.text: Vandalia’s brick state house replaced an unsafe predecessor in 1836. Abraham Lincoln had begun his legislative career in the earlier building in 1834; he returned in autumn 1836 to the new one. In February 1837, the legislature voted to move the capital to Springfield, which took over in 1839. Vandalia’s building became the county courthouse and served that role until 1933. The porticoes belong to that later chapter: added in the late 1850s, they gave the Federal-style building its Greek Revival appearance. The state reclaimed it in 1933 and began an extensive program of interior refitting and reconstruction.
